q: A 2-year-old child has a head circumference of 40 cm. All of the following are possible causes EXCEPT:
e: The expected head circumference at 2 years is about 49 cm, so 40 cm is microcephaly. Rickets thickens the skull and causes a large head, not a small one.

q: Recognized causes of macrocephaly include all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Down syndrome causes a small head (microcephaly with brachycephaly). Thalassaemia and achondroplasia thicken or enlarge the skull; hydrocephalus and megalencephaly enlarge its contents.

q: All of the following are causes of macrocephaly EXCEPT:
e: Down syndrome is a chromosomal cause of microcephaly. The other options cause macrocephaly.

q: Regarding normal weight change in a child, all are true EXCEPT:
o: Weight loss occurs in the first few days of life
Birth weight is regained by 10–14 days
Weight gain is about 2 kg/year after 2 years
e: The birth weight doubles at 4–5 months and triples at 1 year.

q: A full-term infant doubles the birth weight by:
e: An infant gains about ¾ kg per month in the first 4 months, so a 3 kg baby weighs about 6 kg at 4–5 months.

q: The average growth of head circumference during the first year of life is:
e: The head circumference grows from 35 cm at birth to 47 cm at 1 year: 2 cm per month for 3 months, 1 cm per month for 3 months and 0.5 cm per month for 6 months.

q: How much does the length of a baby increase in the first year?
e: The length increases from 50 cm at birth to 75 cm at 1 year.

q: All of the following measurements are true EXCEPT:
o: Head circumference is 35 cm at birth
Weight of a term infant doubles by 4–5 months
e: The length is 75 cm at 1 year; 100 cm is reached at about 4 years.

q: A child's head circumference and length are both on the 10th centile and have stayed there on serial visits. The best interpretation is:
e: Measurements between −2 and +2 standard deviations (the 3rd to 97th centile) that follow their own channel are normal.

q: Which statement about growth is true?
o: Head growth velocity decreases with advancing age
A baby born at 3 kg will be 12 kg at 1 year
The posterior fontanelle closes at 18 months
Boys reach peak height velocity before girls
e: The head circumference grows by 12 cm in the first year and by only about 2 cm in the second year. A baby born at 3 kg weighs about 9 kg at 1 year.

q: Delayed bone age with failure to grow is most typical of:
e: Hypothyroidism delays the bone age the most. Familial short stature has a normal bone age, and the other options advance it.

q: Teething (eruption of the first tooth) normally starts at:
e: The first tooth, a lower central incisor, erupts at about 6 months. No tooth by 13 months is delayed teething.

q: Which of the following causes microcephaly?
e: Trisomy 21 is a chromosomal cause of microcephaly; the other options cause a large head.

q: A 4-year-old boy needs a drug dose but cannot be weighed. His estimated weight is:
e: For children aged 1–6 years, weight (kg) = (age in years × 2) + 8 = 16 kg.

q: The growth indicator that best reflects chronic (long-standing) undernutrition is:
e: A low height-for-age (stunting) reflects chronic undernutrition. A low weight-for-height (wasting) and a low MUAC reflect acute undernutrition.

q: An 18-month-old child has a MUAC of 11 cm with no oedema. This indicates:
e: In children aged 6–59 months, a mid-upper arm circumference below 11.5 cm is severe acute malnutrition.

q: A 10-month-old girl's weight fell from the 50th to below the 5th centile; length is on the 10th and head circumference on the 50th centile. The most likely group of causes is:
e: In undernutrition the weight falls first and the length later, and the head is spared until late. In endocrine disease the height falls first.

q: A 6-month-old born at 30 weeks is below the 5th centile for weight, length and head circumference on the term chart. Development is normal for corrected age. The next step is to:
e: Preterm infants are plotted at their corrected age until 2 years. At the corrected age, his growth is normal.

q: The anterior fontanelle normally closes at:
e: The anterior fontanelle closes at 12–18 months and the posterior fontanelle by 2 months.

q: A late-closing anterior fontanelle is seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
e: Craniosynostosis closes the fontanelle early. The other options cause a large or late-closing fontanelle.
